When the Market Punishes "Perfection": A Harsh Lesson from the 2025 Bottom In the markets, the spotlight is always on the winners. But true wisdom always lurks in the "losers' list." The worst-performing companies in the S&P 500 for 2025 aren't bankrupt companies, but rather giants that everyone thought were invincible. Here's what this list tells us about the market's psychology this year. 1. The Freefall of "Growth Stocks" When companies like The Trade Desk ($TTD) and Fiserv ($FISV) lose nearly 67% of their value in a single year, it means one thing: "The valuation bubble has burst." The market is no longer forgiving companies that price themselves as "perfect." Any slight slowdown in growth is met with collective punishment. Investors have fled the "promises of tomorrow" in fintech and advertising. -- 2. Consumers Close Their Wallets Look at the names: Lululemon ($LULU): -45.7% Chipotle ($CMG): -38.6% Target ($TGT): -27.7% These companies were symbols of consumer power. Lululemon no longer sells a "lifestyle" but rather expensive clothing in a time of austerity. And Chipotle is no longer the easy lunch option. The message is clear: Consumers in 2025 are very price-sensitive, and companies that relied solely on "brand" have paid the price. -- 3. Even “Defense” Didn’t Protect You The biggest surprise is the presence of consumer staples (Staples) and healthcare companies: Clorox ($CLX): -37.9% UnitedHealth ($UNH): -34.7% General Mills ($GIS): -27.1% We usually look to these stocks as a safe haven. But when these defensive stocks fall this hard, it often indicates a structural change (perhaps pressure on profit margins or rising debt costs). - The Bottom Line: Mean Reversion This list is a reminder of a timeless financial principle: “A tree doesn’t grow to the sky.” The stocks that soared in 2023 and 2024 crashed back down in 2025. Financial intelligence isn’t about chasing up, but about knowing when the “beautiful story” is becoming too expensive. If you want to buy a guitar and it’s $850… The way my mind works is to think, “I have to work 17 hours to buy that?” Or, in wider terms, extrapolate that to a vacation. Say for a family of 4 to go to Disney for 5 days. Let’s say all in its $8,000 for 5 days? So I’d have to work 160 hours (or 20 days) to spend 5 overpriced days at a subpar attraction? Instead of considering whether something is worth the money, consider is it worth x-amount of your time. As far as pricey items? My dad always asked, “would you buy that if the name wasn’t on the label?” Would you wear it if nobody knew it was YSL or Lululemon? If you buy something that’s expensive for a bargain, do you want people to think you paid the actual or expected price? Because if you do, it’s a brag. These questions have a psychological effect on the buyer. Young people are not being taught these things. I like nice things. But I like a bargain more… and I value my time even more than a bargain.

Roewe most sighted car in Shanghai vs BYD in Beijing, XPeng in Guangzhao etc. Plenty of Tesla's on roads in all cities. Spotted some YYYs. - Can't go without Alipay. Curt Cignetti will soon sign a new contract with Indiana that pays him at least $12.5 million per year. But after digging into the numbers, Cignetti might still be the most undervalued coach in college football (and not for the reason you might think). We all know what Cignetti has done at IU is remarkable — he turned a perennial cellar-dweller into the national championship favorite just two years after his arrival. This has transformed IU's athletic department: • Before the 2025 season even kicked off, ticket revenue for IU's football team had surpassed $13 million. • Indiana announced a $50 million stadium naming rights deal with Merchants Bank. • Fundraising has hit a record high, with billionaire IU alum Mark Cuban donating to the athletic department for the first time ever. But that's the obvious stuff; Cignetti's real impact comes in the admissions office. IU's football team is essentially a marketing vehicle for the university — 24 million people watched them win the Rose Bowl, 18 million watched them win the Big Ten Championship, and when College Gameday visited Indiana's campus last year, more than 2 million people watched a 3-hour commercial about the school. This publicity is worth hundreds of millions of dollars and is having a real impact on Indiana's finances. In 2025 alone, Indiana University set school records for total enrollment (48,626 students), freshman class size (10,127 students), first-year out-of-state students (4,697), and application volume (73,400). Indiana University Applicants • 2019-20: 44,178 • 2020-21: 46,623 • 2021-22: 50,159 • 2022-23: 54,345 • 2023-24: 67,731 • 2024-25: 73,400 But since IU can only admit so many students each year, they leverage the additional demand to 1) rotate the composition of their student body toward out-of-state students, and 2) become more selective academically. Out-of-state students now account for about 50% of IU's total enrollment, with the school admitting a total of 4,697 new out-of-state students in 2025 — roughly 500 more out-of-state students than IU's previous record. This is an important distinction because out-of-state students pay $30,000 more in annual tuition – $12,000 for Indiana residents versus $42,000 for non-residents. 500 new out-of-state students x $30,000 tuition difference ––––––––– = $15 million annually If you multiply that by a four-year degree, these out-of-state students are worth $60 million more to IU than their in-state counterparts. And since football success attracts more applicants, IU's admissions office can be more selective. Indiana's Fall 2025 class had a median high school GPA of 3.94 — the highest in IU admissions history. This creates a virtuous cycle. Better sports → more applicants → better students → higher rankings. Higher rankings then lead to even more applicants, and, eventually, higher tuition revenues. This is exactly what happened at Alabama with Nick Saban, and it's a big reason why Indiana is completely comfortable giving Cignetti new contracts every year. P.S. Year 7 of Covid. My mother needed to return a final sale item. In store returns only for final sale items. I also had a gift card I wanted to use. So we went to the mall outside New Orleans. A known respiratory illness hotspot right now. I used to love malls. I don’t anymore. I have Long Covid. And over time, my body learned something my mind didn’t ask for. I can feel it when Covid is nearby. When someone is infected. Not anxiety. Not imagination. A physical alarm. I was fine in the car. Fine walking in. Then I stepped into the Lululemon dressing room. I just needed to make sure the shirt fit before I spent my gift card. Instant nose itch. Pressure flooding my ears. Eyes burning. That familiar warning. I rushed frantically, hands shaking, pulling fabric over my head. It fit. I needed to leave. As I stepped out, I heard it. A woman coughing hard. Wet. Uncontrolled. Standing inches away, browsing leggings like nothing was wrong. That’s where the warning I had came from I assumed nervously. Later, passing the food court, I turned my head to look. It was packed. And my vision became blurred. Eyes on fire burning. Vertigo hit so hard I almost collapsed. Nose screaming with the tingly itching. We moved fast to get by. The last hit came in line for coffee. I planned on bringing the coffee out to the car to enjoy it on the way home. The back of my throat started burning and felt dry and scratchy. Ears became full again. That awful question looping in my mind as my eyes scanned the area: Who is it? Who is infected here? We made it back to the car. We escaped. I began to enjoy my coffee. But I miss the old world. I miss not being able to panic everywhere I go. Covid didn’t just take health. It took safety away in ordinary places. I live inside a body that no longer trusts the world. It listens constantly. It detects danger while others feel nothing. There is no true rest for me. Only the tension of waiting for the next invisible threat to pass close enough to trigger the alarm. What people call a 6th sense is not a gift to me. It’s a survival reflex burned into me by repeated harm. A curse that wakes with me, walks with me, and never sleeps. Even when I desperately need it to.

In that way, it does represent another side of Israel. Ramat Aviv is a neighborhood in northwest Tel Aviv, Israel. Ramat Aviv is bordered by Einstein Street in the north, Chaim Levanon Street to the east and south, and Namir Road in the west. The main streets in the neighborhood are Brodetzki and Reading. In the neighborhood are the Alliance High School and Ramat Aviv Mall. In the northeast of the neighborhood, opposite university campus, are student dorms of Tel Aviv University. Landmarks opposite the roads bordering the neighborhood are the main campus of Tel Aviv University, the Eretz Israel Museum, the Palmach Museum, and Beth Hatefutsoth. Ramat Aviv was founded in 1950s following the great influx of immigrants from Eastern Europe. Golda Meir lived in the neighborhood from 1959 to 1978. Remains of a Samaritan synagogue were uncovered in Ramat Aviv and first reported in 1978 by archaeologist Haya Kaplan. The structure is dated to the early 7th century CE. The site yielded several mosaic inscriptions: one in Samaritan script naming two donors, and two in Greek — a donor inscription and a blessing on Israel and the house of worship. In January 2011 it was published that remains of a building, believed to be 7,800–8,400 years old, were discovered in an archaeological excavation carried out in 8 Fichman Street in Ramat Aviv, by the Israel Antiquities Authority. The findings attest to permanent habitation on the northern bank of the Yarkon River. The official name of the Ramat Aviv mall is Kenyon Ofer but it is well known as Ramat Aviv Mall. There are chain stores and boutiques, the premium international shops consist of names such as: Louis Vuitton, Carolina Hererra, H.Stern, Steve Madden, American Eagle. There, officers found an unoccupied vehicle matching the description of the one the offenders fled in and saw Lululemon merchandise in plain view inside. Officers canvassed the area and located 20-year-old Jadea Seals near a dumpster in an alley in the 200 block of Green Street. Podcast Summary | Call Her Daddy: Sarah J Maas: The Wait Is Over Overview Sarah J. Maas, author of the massively popular Throne of Glass, A Court of Thorns and Roses, and Crescent City series, details her journey from a discouraged teenage writer to a literary powerhouse with over 75 million books sold. She reveals the profound personal traumas, including a traumatic emergency C-section and a mental health crisis, that have directly shaped her narratives, moving beyond the "smut" label to explore themes of survival, empowerment, and authentic female experience. Maas asserts complete creative control over her work, from rejecting compromise in future adaptations to defying publishing norms with her upcoming, uniquely structured ACOTAR releases, framing success as the freedom to tell her stories exactly as she envisions them. Key Themes - Creative control is non-negotiable for Maas, who views adaptations as core to her legacy and will reject any changes made for demographic appeal or that deviate from her vision. - Her writing is a channeled, emotional process where she physically embodies her characters, with major plotlines and character arcs emerging directly from her personal trauma, therapy, and growth. - She intentionally writes authentic, relatable fantasy for women by including "the real stuff" like bodily functions and complex motherhood, rejecting the dismissal of her work as "just smut" as a sexist double standard. - Maas’s career is a story of defiant independence, overcoming near-universal early rejection and discouragement from family and academia to build a universe where her series now converge as planned. - Success is defined as creative freedom and personal happiness, not just sales, with a mindset focused on long-term storytelling on her own terms rather than external validation. Detailed Summary Sarah J. Maas writes from a personal, joyful space in her bedroom at a tidy desk adorned with crystals and a Lululemon bag. Her process involves specific rituals, like requiring three coasters for different drinks and snacking on Flamin’ Hot Cheetos. Inspiration comes from soundtracks played on vinyl, including the 2022 "Batman" score and music from "Demon Slayer." This controlled environment fuels a writing method she describes as almost supernatural, where plot elements align as if from a "humanwide psychic thing" and she physically cries while channeling her characters' emotions. Her path to this point was fiercely independent. As a teenager, she shifted from assigned "boring" school books to self-discovered fantasy, a passion she kept secret alongside an anime love for Sailor Moon. She began writing Throne of Glass at 16 on floppy disks using a square iMac as an escape from an unhappy high school experience. Despite material support from her lawyer parents, including an unlimited book budget, they were skeptical of her publishing prospects. This discouragement was echoed by a creative writing MFA director who visibly dismissed her for writing fantasy. Maas resisted all traditional literary training, insisting on writing her chosen genre from the start. This defiance shaped her career. She faced near-universal rejection, with every agent and publisher except one initially saying no. She wrote the first two ACOTAR books in about two months in 2008 while waiting for responses on Throne of Glass. Crescent City began as a private, unpublished passion project for creative play, featuring more cursing, with no initial plan to publish. All three major series were designed to converge, a complex architecture developed over many years starting very early in her career. Maas strongly rejects the reductive label of "smut" or "romantic fantasy." She argues this is a sexist double standard where any inclusion of sexuality by women authors leads to the devaluation of their entire work. For her, sexual content is "intensely tied to their own emotional journeys" and character development. She points to fans who credit A Court of Mist and Fury with inspiring them to leave abusive relationships, not just for the "hot scenes." She intentionally writes "the real stuff," including bodily functions like periods, to create authentic, relatable fantasy worlds for women. This authenticity is rooted in deep personal experience. Her traumatic emergency C-section with her son, who was two weeks late and in distress, left lasting physical and emotional scars. The incision was made "way too high" and "destroyed like the flow and look of my stomach." A male doctor yelled at her for eating before the procedure, and only a med school intern showed her kindness. She believes she and her son would have died a century earlier. A later gynecologist reacted with anger to the scar, calling it "unnecessary" and the result of a "lazy" doctor. This trauma directly fed into the emotional core of Feyre's pregnancy storyline, focusing on loss of bodily autonomy. Motherhood as a source of strength and complexity, not a glossed-over "happily ever after," became a key theme. Writing A Court of Silver Flames was intertwined with her own mental health crisis in fall 2019, which involved prolonged panic attacks and a "very dark place" that led her to therapy and medication. She wrote Nesta's emotional arc while actively processing her own trauma; the pivotal scene where Nesta breaks down on a hike was conceived during Maas's own emotional breakdown on a hike in New Zealand. Therapy helped her separate self-worth from professional success. Her therapist had her mentally walk through a scenario where her career was "all done" to prove she would survive. This allowed her to reclaim joy in writing, which had become a stressful "job" due to deadlines, leading to panic attacks. She views her family, husband, and friends as unconditional blessings that "nothing can take away." Her character dynamics often emerge organically. When first writing ACOTAR, she did not plan the plot; the character Rhysand entered a scene unexpectedly, changing the story's direction. She finds irony in early fans getting tattoos of Tamlin before his full controlling arc was revealed. She views Tamlin's behavior as a result of trauma and lack of emotional tools, not pure villainy, but does not excuse actions like locking Feyre in the manor. She is conflicted about a potential redemption arc, weighing narrative exploration against validating readers who saw their own abusive relationships in him. Maas believes characters in relationships must maintain autonomy and equality, a non-negotiable principle. She intentionally writes main characters like Rhysand to make serious mistakes from a place of love and fear, creating realistic conflict. Rhysand's failure to fully communicate the risks of Feyre's pregnancy is framed as a "bad call" made from terror, informed by his inexperience despite being over 500 years old. The most romantic moment between them, the Starfall scene, was inspired by Florence and the Machine's "Cosmic Love." Chapter 55 of Silver Flames is cited as a major emotional release, a culmination of long-built backstory that required little editing. The concept of "mates" in her series explores the tension between biological destiny and free will. She finds the tension of an unwanted bond a compelling challenge. The next ACOTAR book is confirmed for release on October 27th, noting it took time due to personal life events and finding the right story. This upcoming story defies traditional publishing. It is one massive narrative split into four parts, with Part 1 alone at approximately 400 pages. The full story is over a thousand pages across three physical volumes. The first part releases October 27th, with the next installment (Parts 2 & 3 combined) on January 12th. This back-to-back schedule is to avoid making fans wait. The project was written quickly after a creative block broke during a stay in Montana. She is currently editing two massive books simultaneously, prioritizing the organic needs of the story over industry rules. Looking forward, Maas asserts complete creative control over any future TV or film adaptations, rejecting changes made for demographic appeal. She will not compromise on casting, citing an ongoing search for the "perfect" actor for a character like Rhysand. She has reclaimed the rights to all her literary works, a significant professional shift. She defines success as the creative freedom to tell stories on her own terms combined with personal happiness. She maintains a long-term mindset, originally willing to publish even one book in her lifetime. She rejects external doubt as motivation, responding to being told she "couldn't do something" with a defiant "Watch me." On series futures, she confirms Bryce and Hunt from Crescent City are endgame, dismissing fan theories about Bryce and Azriel. A Throne of Glass book project was set aside as it required more time than currently available. She has 3-4 unpublished full books for different series on her computer that may never be released. She included otters in Crescent City simply because she loves them. Her fan interactions remain deeply personal; she often approaches readers in public to thank them and sometimes interrupts their reading to discuss the book, viewing the connection as the ultimate reward for her defiant, authentic, and emotionally charged creative journey. The growth of my social media account and root of my legitimacy is purely in the fact that I know how the ruling classes in Britain, Italy, and the United States dressed during the 20th century. When Vivek Ramaswamy and Pete Hegseth wear tan shoes with navy suits, I can say "this looks like shit to most people because it's not how King Charles and Gianni Agenlli would have dressed." When Kash Patel puts contrast buttonholes on his suits, I can say it's wrong because the ruling classes across these countries during that period would have never chosen such a thing. You read this as legitimate purely because you accept the legitimacy of these classes in forming our sense of aesthetics. Someone who has no interest in these classes — such as Paul Harden and Yohji Yamamoto — rightly disregards all of these notions and makes tailoring according to different rules. The polo shirt is no different. The spread of the polo shirt is a story about how a pullover garment migrated from the polo fields played by British imperialists to tennis legends in France and eventually to the golfing middle classes in the United States. This is entirely a story about race, class, and gender. Football jerseys and basketball shorts don't enjoy such history, and thus they are not seen as legitimate business clothes. The difference between me and other menswear writers is that: 1) I make this history and dynamic transparent and 2) I don't think the white upper class are the sole source for cultural legitimacy. There are many legitimate aesthetics that have nothing to do with this class, such as biker gear, workwear, punk and rap aesthetics, etc. I just think it's weird to shit on contemporary women's athleisure while wearing a polo shirt, one of the original pieces of athleisure, albeit primarily worn by upper class white men.

This is an email mistake any ecommerce brand can make easily, without even noticing. Here's how to not end up like LululemonLululemon was fined for sending marketing emails without an unsubscribe link. In most countries, the law differentiates between "marketing" and "transactional" emails. Transactional emails include important information like receipts, order confirmations, etc. Whereas marketing emails pitch products and promotions. Popular ecommerce ESPs (like Klaviyo) sometimes DO NOT include unsubscribe links in transactional emails by default (in many cases, unsubscribe links are only legally required for marketing emails). Based on the article, it appears Lululemon put "marketing content" into their "transactional" emails. That's what exposed them to the fines. Had they sent the exact same content in a separate marketing automation where their ESP included the unsubscribe link, the same content would have been sent legally.

Lululemon: A Compounding Machine on Sale 
$LULU
 This is not a company in trouble. It just looks like one. Lululemon's stock is down over 50% from its peak. The market has repriced it like a struggling retailer — but the fundamentals tell a different story. Return on equity sits at 41%, ROIC at 33%, and the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.39. Those are not the numbers of a broken business. They're the numbers of a brand-compounding machine that temporarily disappointed Wall Street's growth expectations. The Discount Is Real LULU's EV/EBITDA is currently ~6.8x — roughly 69% below its 10-year median of 22x. The trailing P/E of ~12x compares to a 10-year historical average above 40x. You are buying the same business — same margins, same brand moat, same loyal customer base — at a fraction of what it commanded two years ago. Why Is It Cheap? The selloff stems from a genuine but likely temporary deceleration. North American same-store growth slowed, the CEO departure created uncertainty, and macro pressure on discretionary spending hit sentiment hard. Mr. Market conflated a growth slowdown with a structural collapse. He was wrong before with Nike, Starbucks, and Chipotle. He's probably wrong here too. Why It's Worth Owning Lululemon has something most retailers never build: a customer whoidentifies with the brand. The repurchase rate, the pricing power, the $100 leggings that never go on sale — these are signs of a true consumer franchise. The share count has also dropped nearly 4% in one year, meaning management is quietly buying back stock at these depressed prices. That's a green flag. At 6.8x EBITDA, you're not paying for perfection. You're paying for pessimism. That's the deep value entry.

Textile Robot Skin Turns Fabric into a Nervous System Robot skin is getting touchier. The Chinese company JQ Industries just introduced a fabric-based electronic skin (e-skin) to give robots a humanlike sense of touch. Made from plant-derived materials, it behaves like fabric and can bend and conform like clothing without restricting movement. So basically, Lululemon with embedded sensors. The skin is woven with conductive fibers that detect pressure, contact and force distribution. The system uses sensor gloves for the hands and pressure-sensing soles for the feet. The E-skin acts as a distributed nervous system. It transmits data from thousands of sensing points to the robot’s artificial intelligence for instant decision-making. It integrates with simulation environments like NVIDIA Isaac Sim and MuJoCo for training AI models using tactile feedback. Shanghai-based JQ Industries demonstrated the capabilities using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, but the technology is intended for use across platforms. The company says the enhanced sensitivity unlocks more precise grip control and better handling of delicate objects. They say it also makes robots safer around humans. JQ’s ultimate goal is to create a closed loop so next-gen robots can learn from touch the same way humans do. JQ says its technology differs from traditional electronic skin that relies on delicate thin film that’s hard to produce and tends to degrade with bending. It’s produced with textile manufacturing techniques like modified industrial weaving and roll-to-roll production. Launched in early 2024, JQ Industries operates as Weihai Juqiao Industrial Technology. The early-stage startup is scaling production of the tactile-sensing technology with at least $2.8 million raised to date.

The AG's investigation targets PFAS ("forever chemicals" like PFOA/PFOS) in Lululemon activewear. Independent lab tests (e.g., Mamavation 2021, CEH studies) have detected them in leggings/sports bras from Lululemon and similar brands. Lululemon uses PFAS for water/stain/sweat resistance—enhancing performance in high-activity gear (repels oils/moisture better than alternatives). It's not just profit; it improves durability/function. The company has a Restricted Substances List phasing them out since 2021, but trace levels persist in some supply chains. PFAS are persistent and linked to health risks (endocrine disruption, immune effects, cancer in high exposures per EPA/NIH data). Dermal absorption from clothing is real (studies show sweat amplifies uptake), but lower than ingestion via water/food. No acute harm from casual wear, but long-term concern for frequent users—especially if sweating heavily. Consumers should check labels for "PFAS-free" claims as brands reformulate.

Lululemon doesn't just sell yoga pants. They sell the identity of someone who sweats, grows, and connects. For example, their ambassador program isn't celebrities. It's local yoga instructors, studio owners, community runners. These are real people in your neighborhood who host free classes and embody the "sweatlife." This way, when you wear Lululemon you don't feel like a customer. You feel like you belong to something. And that same psychology is why most google display and demand gen ads completely miss. Most brands run ads like this: "Premium yoga pants. 4-way stretch. Shop now." Feature → feature → CTA → nobody cares. Instead, your ads should look more like this: A photo of a group mid-class, real people, real sweat. Copy that says "trusted by 50,000 local movers" or "join the community." The difference is belonging vs buying. People don't click because they need another pair of leggings. They click because they want to be the kind of person wearing those leggings. And when your ad signals that other people like them already chose your brand, it removes the risk and adds the identity appeal at the same time. This is in-group bias and it works in demand gen and display campaigns because those placements are inherently visual and emotional, not transactional. So show your customers using the product, not just the product. Add social proof that signals community. Your creative should make someone feel like they're joining something. Not just buying something. - Daniel

Half the names trading at 52-week lows today are blue-chip compounders. The other half are structurally broken. Retail can't tell the difference until it's too late. The reality is that 52-week lows mean nothing without the why. Mastercard and Visa are weak because of stablecoin substitution risk and EU interchange caps. Both are temporary regulatory headwinds, not structural breaks. Buy. Adobe and Salesforce are weak because the market believes generative AI commoditizes their workflow tools. The bear thesis has been wrong for 18 months and the businesses keep printing 11-15% growth. Buy if you have a 24-month timeline. Nike, Lululemon, Chipotle, McDonald's are weak because consumer discretionary is bleeding. GLP-1 demand destruction in fast food, China consumer slowdown for Nike, post-pandemic mean reversion for Chipotle and Lulu. Wait. These need 1-2 more quarters to bottom. UNH is weak because the DOJ has open criminal and civil investigations. Avoid until the settlement. Novo Nordisk is weak because GLP-1 competition from Lilly is structurally worse for NVO every quarter. Avoid. Kraft Heinz, General Mills, P&G, Kimberly-Clark are weak because private label is taking share at every grocery store in America. Structural, not cyclical. Avoid. Sea Limited, MELI, Toast, TTD, Figma are weak because high-growth multiples got compressed industry-wide. These are the asymmetric setups in the list. Buy with conviction. A 52-week low is a question, not an answer. The question is whether the company is being punished for what's broken or for what's misunderstood. Get that wrong and you catch knives. Get it right and you compound.

A few research-based points on the Lululemon saga: 1) Board and governance dynamics are fascinating, and board composition matters. Research is pretty clear on the fact that board characteristics affect CEO choice and strategic outcomes, although there are many factors involved here. My research-based take on what's happening is that we have a board that is reasonably cohesive, connected, powerful, yet perhaps lacking the diversity and direct expertise that Lululemon needs. Studies suggest that may lead to what we are observing through some distinct but interdependent channels: A) Especially in the face of underperformance, such boards may prioritize consensus, trust, and solidarity instead of seeking new expertise and novel solutions. Redundancy and conservatism, rather than true synergy and search for novel solutions and expertise, is the likely outcome. The end result is a more reactive than a proactive board. B) Along similar lines, some research would suggest there may be a case of pluralistic ignorance here, where board members on a cohesive, comfortable board that lacks the right diversity may individually perceive the need for more change, yet jointly underestimate the others' perceived need for strategic change, resulting in consensus around lukewarm strategic decisions that do not go far enough. C) Boards with long-tenured directors, and directors with similar background, capabilities, and social capital work better for mature, stable, well-performing firms, which doesn't seem to be the case here. Entrenched, powerful, less diverse boards and boards lacking right diversity also tend to choose CEOs that fit their own profile. 2) And yes, generally, board dynamics aside, I am also puzzled by the CEO choice, as is the market. If you’re early in business and not yet large, don’t feel bad. The things all great builders have? Time in the game. All the greats are honest about it. Nike, ~15 years to $100M (founded as Blue Ribbon Sports in 1964, crossed $100M around fiscal 1979). Phil Knight ran the mile at Oregon, then did his Stanford MBA, where he wrote a paper arguing Japanese running shoes could do to Adidas what Japanese cameras did to Leica. Twelve years of running and thinking about running before founding day. His co-founder Bill Bowerman was his old Oregon coach, sixteen years into coaching at the school, already a legend for hand-cobbling shoes for his runners and obsessively re-soling Tigers in his garage. Bowerman had been thinking about shoe construction for two decades by the time they shook hands. Please read Show Dog. It’s a foundational book for me on entrepreneurship. Starbucks, ~22 years (founded 1971, crossed $100M around 1993). The original three (Jerry Baldwin, Zev Siegl, Gordon Bowker) were a teacher, a teacher, and a writer. They’d been roasting and selling beans for fifteen years before the company really moved. The sprint belongs to Howard Schultz, and he wasn’t a coffee guy either. Brooklyn public housing kid, football scholarship to Northern Michigan, three grinding years selling word processors at Xerox door-to-door, then five years at Hammarplast selling Swedish kitchenware (which is how he stumbled onto Starbucks as a customer). Apple, ~4 years (founded April 1976, $118M in the fiscal year ending September 1980). Wozniak, 25, had been designing circuits since he was 11. He’d been at HP for a few years building calculators, but more importantly he’d spent every Wednesday at the Homebrew Computer Club showing his designs to other obsessives. Roughly fifteen years of self-taught hardware work. Jobs, 21, was the green one: Reed dropout, a few months at Atari, a trip to India. Lululemon, ~7-8 years (founded 1998, crossed $100M in fiscal 2006). Chip Wilson, 42 at founding, had nineteen years in technical apparel behind him. He’d started Westbeach in 1979 making surf shorts, watched the surf market die, pivoted to skate, watched that fade, pivoted to snowboard outerwear, built it to ~$15M, and sold in 1997. He was already a seasoned operator before lululemon Feastables (MrBeast), $33M year one, $96M year two, $250M year three. Jimmy started uploading at 13 under MrBeast6000, mostly Minecraft and Call of Duty commentary. He spent five years uploading to nobody, dropped out of community college, until “I counted to 100,000” broke through in 2017. By the time Feastables launched in January 2022, he’d been on the platform for ten years and had become the most-subscribed creator on Earth. Disney, ~42 years to $100M (founded 1923, hit ~$110M in 1965). Walt was 21 at founding but had been drawing for money since he was a teenager: ad work in Kansas City, his own studio Laugh-O-Gram (bankrupt within two years), then a one-way train ticket to Hollywood with $40 in his pocket. Sixish years of failing in animation before Disney Brothers Studio. Under Armour (Kevin Plank), ~7 years to $100M (founded 1996). Plank was 24 at founding. He’d run a flower delivery business in high school, sold roses on Valentine’s Day in college dorms, then ran a t-shirt company called Cupid’s Valentine that he used to fund himself through Maryland. Eight years of small-scale entrepreneurship plus four years sweating through cotton tees as a walk-on football player. he knew how to sell things out of a trunk because he’d been doing it since 17.

Can We Admit That Low IQ People Exist? There are different classes of people. Different cognitive bands. Different capabilities. Some are smarter, some are simpler. They tend to congregate into groups. Saying this out loud makes you a monster, but I'm saying it because we all know it’s true. And it is: IQ distributions are bell curves. The middle of the curve, the part most of us live in, sits between roughly 85 and 115. About two-thirds of people are in there. The other third splits into the tails. One tail noticeably below the middle, one tail noticeably above. The shape of the curve is not contested. The honesty about what it means is contested. I worked this out at Meatstock - a meat festival that tours Australia, and a ‘Destruction Derby’ at a rural racetrack. I’m talking about authentic events, in rural environments. Not your typical urban show where the country comes to the city. A different sort of human goes to these rural shows. Meatstock came to Lardner Park, an hour and a half southeast of Melbourne. It’s an open plains area, the kind of paddock that runs cattle eleven months of the year and trade shows on the twelfth. The Sydney version of Meatstock runs at Olympic Park: modern, urban, and surrounded by professionals living in medium density townhouses. The Melbourne version runs in a paddock, and the crowd it draws is not the crowd that turns up at Olympic Park. I rolled in wearing a 2XU tracksuit, thinking I was toning down my usual edgy athleisure style (Lululemon etc). I thought leaving the Volvo XC40 at home and taking the Ford Ranger with the bull bar and all terrains was not just a wise weather and terrain choice but would also help me fit in. To appear less of a city slicker. Turns out, my tracksuit was too nice, my car was too shiny, and my brain was too high functioning. The thing is, I am not a city slicker. I farm. I run cattle. I spend all day tensioning barbed wire. I scrape cow poo off my face after it flings off tractor tyres and into my eyes. I know more about welding, farming, fencing and machinery than most people who walked past me at Meatstock and Destruction Derby. Many of them were neckbeards with a caravan. Their bodies screamed the evidence of a lifetime of sedentary video gaming and TV watching, not trades or farming. They must love meat as much as I do! Despite my efforts at dressing down, it wasn’t enough to fit in. I also had to translate myself: A singer-songwriter was singing on stage, performing a country song with a presentation that contradicted her lyrics, a pretty obvious artistic move. Sometimes her songs would back-to-back conflict with each other in psychological framing. Another fascinating insight inter her tapestry of personality and life experience. Other times she’d make typical stage-remarks we are all used to: ‘you’re singing so well’, despite nobody singing. Then she’d display remarkable authenticity and vulnerability by admitting to and owning errors wholeheartedly. What a captivating display of emotional and cognitive performance, tension and contradiction in real time! I wondered why she would cover over some things, and expose others. Did she want to signal transparency? Or polish? Or both – and why? What drove her in those fleeting moments of micro-decision? But I couldn't say a word about any of this. Not because the people around me would have disagreed. Because they would have been embarrassed. Can you imagine if I turned to the friendly neckbeard in the VB shirt next to me and remarked on the cognitive dissonance of the performer, wondering whether she was experiencing a fluctuating confidence state as her set unfolded? Would he even understand the concept of cognitive dissonance? Or was I simply revealing my prejudice, assuming his lower cognitive ability? It didn’t matter. I couldn’t take the chance. I believe the observation itself would have made him feel exposed. Stupid. Big words, big concepts, wholly inappropriate for the setting. So I held it all in. The same thing happened at the Destruction Derby I attended in a similar rural setting. There appeared to be some kind of uniform enforcement because everyone was wearing all black. Black jeans, black shirts, the occasional heavy metal or beer logo. Not charcoal. Not grey. No colour, no stripes, no patterns. Just solid black. And all the same – black jeans and hoodies. Maybe the local Kmart didn’t stock any other style. I overheard their conversations as we sat on the grass, with my highly paid and credentialed doctor friends, who attended with me. My wife heard them too, sitting in her classic sundress. We stuck out like we didn’t belong, because we didn’t. The banter I overheard proved as much. The things they said around me were not stupid, just visceral. Simple and without abstraction. They were running at full capacity in their register, open and authentic with their friends and family. Direct, grounded, and fluent but certainly not abstract. Not cognitively challenging. Not at all curious, just statements of observation and fact. Never a question. At both Meatstock and at Destruction Derby, I was the one shedding cognitive load to fit in and meet everyone where they were at. And I had to shed a lot. This is the part nobody wants to admit. There are different classes. There are different cognitive bands. The people I was around genuinely could not have processed an abstraction about staging psychology or daytime-versus-nighttime audience framing, or fashion semiotics. I was certain they didn’t notice their communal uniform and the group dynamics that it forces, especially when someone fails to comply. But I did. Not because they are lazy or undereducated. They may be those things – I don’t know – but more critically is that a cognitive operation isn't one they run in their head. They run others. They run trucks, they run brisket pits, they run fencing rigs and chainsaws and welding gear. They run social cues and hierarchies unconsciously, and probably claim them to be ‘self-evident’. Except they’re not self-evident. Just like any other human group or class, they were taking part in a sociological ritual, their decision making shunted toward particular paths. And here's the move most people make, and the move I refuse to make: Most people, having admitted the cognitive gap, immediately reach for a balancing equation: ‘Sure, they can't think like me, a lawyer, but I can't milk a cow, so…’ This is a cheap admission. It's pity dressed as humility. It pretends the two capabilities are equivalent, that the ledger balances out, that nobody is actually behind on anything because we're all just specialists. That’s not true. And that's not what I saw. I saw that they were genuinely behind in abstraction and cognitive depth. Genuinely. And it doesn’t matter, but not for the weak reason I just explained some people reach for. It doesn’t matter because their worth doesn't rest on it. Worth is not stored in cognitive horsepower. Worth is not stored in earning potential or vocabulary range or analytical capacity, or urban worldliness. It's stored somewhere else entirely. In being made, in being human, in being here. The capability gap is real but the worth gap is not. The problem comes when you notice a capability difference and then erroneously conclude that you are ‘better’ than someone else. That you are worth more than they are. You’re not. Once you can hold both ledgers separately, the whole tension relaxes. You can look at someone genuinely less cognitively able than you, poorer than you, less experienced than you, less aware than you, and still not need to flatter them, rebalance the ledger, or manufacture a counter-skill that proves they're really your equal. In some domains, they are not your equal. In fact, cumulatively, they might be objectively less useful than you. They may be less intelligent than you. They may be less valuable to the capitalist system than you. Their entire table of talents may be smaller than yours. But that still doesn’t touch their dignity, moral worth, right to a vote and a voice (no matter how uneducated). I really enjoyed Meatstock and the Destruction Derby. I enjoyed the conversations with stall holders and the guy who won the award for best mullet. Top bloke. Sure, I had to park my brain for most of the day but accepting that this was a realm I would never be understood in, and our minds would never meet, was a relief. Maybe I’m smarter than them. I don’t know. Maybe they’re ‘physically’ smarter than me, at practical things. I don’t know. It doesn’t matter. I’m not balancing the ledger anymore. I’m telling the truth. Low IQ people exist. So what?

Jay Icon shouted about racial profiling as they fled. Undeterred, they hit another store nearby. This time, police were waiting. Officers arrested them and searched their hotel room, discovering 12 suitcases crammed with $50,000 in stolen Lululemon gear. Facing serious charges of organized retail theft and fraud, both took plea deals. Their glittering online empire crumbled, leaving them to await sentencing behind bars. I knew they were wrong, but it took an enormous level of confidence to move forward, because I was young and untested, and had never really defied my family like that. Thank goodness I did. That is the cleanest way to read the Chip Wilson proxy fight: not nostalgia, not founder drama, but a live fight over who gets to define the brand now. Lululemon is urging holders to reject Wilson’s director slate — Marc Maurer, Laura Gentile and Eric Hirshberg — and back its own nominees, Chip Bergh, Esi Eggleston Bracey and Teri List. The board’s message is blunt: Wilson’s perspective is outdated, his campaign is damaging, and putting his nominees in the room would weaken the board and disrupt the incoming CEO’s plan. Wilson is attacking the one thing the market actually pays for. His case is that LULU has drifted from the core consumer and needs sharper merchandising, better store execution, and more spending behind marketing and product development. That is not a random activist checklist. For a premium consumer stock, brand heat is the asset, and when that starts leaking, the P&L usually sees it after the customer already has. His nominees fit that critique: On Holding, ESPN, Activision — less “audit committee polish,” more brand, product, media and consumer engagement. The catch: founder instinct is not the same thing as governance. A founder can be directionally right about the brand and still be the wrong mechanism for public-company control. That is where Lululemon is pressing. The company says settlement talks collapsed after Wilson pushed for three directors of his choosing, including two immediate appointments, plus quarterly meetings with the new CEO. That shifts the question from “does Wilson see the problem?” to “is this a board refresh or a control campaign?” The board has its own credibility issue. It is asking investors to trust the current plan at the exact moment Wilson is arguing the plan already missed the consumer. That is a hard sell if execution does not improve quickly. For shareholders, this is not a clean founder-good, board-bad story. It is a tradeoff between creative aggression and operational stability during a CEO transition. Wilson wants disruption because he thinks stability became complacency. The board wants stability because it thinks disruption could damage the very brand he claims to protect. Bottom line: LULU’s proxy fight is a premium-brand duration test. The winner will not be the side with the better press release. It will be the side that proves it can recover brand heat without breaking the machine.

We’ve talked a lot about SaaS, AI infrastructure, and semis recently. Today, let’s put that aside and talk about U.S. consumer stocks. The real story starts with prices. A couple of years ago, eggs were the crazy one. Anyone who went grocery shopping in the U.S. remembers it. A carton of eggs felt absurdly expensive. Breakfast, baking, family grocery baskets — everything got hit. Now eggs have finally cooled down. But just as consumers got some relief there, beef started moving higher again. Beef is different from eggs. The supply cycle is much slower. You don’t fix cattle supply in a few weeks. It takes time — breeding, feeding, processing, supply rebuilding. So when beef prices rise, that pressure can stick around. It shows up in grocery aisles, fast-food menus, restaurant margins, and eventually company earnings. That’s the real state of U.S. consumption right now: Consumers haven’t stopped spending. But every dollar is being reallocated. Rent, mortgages, car payments, insurance, food, healthcare, and credit card interest take the first bite out of the household budget. What’s left is where consumers make choices: Costco bulk pack or full-price brand? Walmart value aisle or specialty store? McDonald’s value meal or a higher-ticket restaurant? New sneakers now or wait? Home improvement project now or delay? So when people say U.S. consumption is strong, they’re not wrong. And when people say U.S. consumption is weak, they’re also not wrong. The better question is: Where is the money flowing? That’s why consumer stocks are getting interesting again. Walmart and Costco are not just winning because they are cheap. They are becoming default choices for households trying to stretch budgets. Groceries, household goods, pharmacy, bulk purchases, membership value — all in one place. When budgets get tight, consumers may actually rely on these places more, not less. McDonald’s is similar. Beef inflation can pressure margins, but value meals still matter when consumers are watching every dollar. People don’t stop eating. They just become much more careful about what a meal is worth. On the other side, companies like Nike, Lululemon, and Home Depot are in a different position. They are not bad companies. They may still be great long-term brands. But buying full-price sneakers, yoga pants, a sofa, new appliances, or starting a kitchen renovation is easier to delay. When budgets tighten, those purchases get pushed out. So you can’t just say, “This consumer stock is down, so it’s cheap.” A lot of stocks are down for a reason. You still have to ask: Has inventory really cleared? Are margins stabilizing? Is operating cash flow improving? Is free cash flow per share actually coming back? A lower stock price is not the same thing as a bottom. It just earns the right to be studied. The food chain is also fascinating. Falling egg prices help consumers and grocery retailers. A cheaper grocery basket helps Walmart, Costco, Kroger, and anyone trying to reinforce a value perception. But for egg producers, falling egg prices mean the extraordinary profits from the last cycle are normalizing. Beef inflation is the opposite. It hurts consumers and pressures restaurants with beef exposure. If menus get too expensive, traffic can suffer. Chicken has been more stable, which can help certain low-price menus and chicken-focused chains. Same food inflation story. Completely different stock implications. That’s one of the easiest mistakes in consumer investing: You see one macro variable. But by the time it hits company earnings, the impact can be totally different depending on the business model. My framework for consumer stocks right now is simple. First: great companies still need the right price. Walmart, Costco, Visa, Mastercard, McDonald’s — these are strong businesses. But the market already knows that. If the price has already discounted years of good news, the return may not be attractive. Second: cheap companies still need data. Nike, Lululemon, Home Depot, and parts of beverages and alcohol may look more interesting after the selloff. But low valuation is not enough. I want to see inventory, margins, and cash flow improve together. Third: cyclical companies need normalized earnings. Eggs, beef, chicken — these are cycles. You can’t value egg producers using peak egg-price profits. And you can’t permanently punish them using trough conditions either. So the next opportunity in consumer stocks is probably not about betting on a broad U.S. consumer rebound. It’s about dispersion. Who captures pressured household budgets? Who converts revenue into margin and cash flow? Whose stock has not already priced in the good news? Who looks cheap but is not actually fixed yet? The hotter tech gets, the more the market may start looking back at ignored areas where cash flow still exists, share is stable, and valuation has become reasonable again. U.S. consumption has not collapsed. But consumers are getting more selective. The opportunity is not in buying “consumer” as one category. It is in finding where the budget is migrating. I asked GPT to write a parody about living in Palo Alto, and it did a hilarious job. Hilarious because so much of it sounded so true, of course. ”When I first moved to Palo Alto, I made the mistake of assuming people here had jobs. Back where I grew up, if someone asked what you did for a living and you answered, “I’m exploring opportunities in the AI alignment space,” they’d assume you were either unemployed or in prison. Here, it apparently means you have a $40 million valuation and a podcast. I discovered this my first morning at Coupa Cafe, where I stood behind a man ordering something called a “deconstructed turmeric adaptogen cortado.” He wore running shoes that looked orthopedic but cost more than my first car. While waiting for his drink, he casually mentioned to the barista that he was “taking some time between exits.” The barista nodded sympathetically, the way one might respond to news of a difficult divorce. “Oh wow,” she said. “Good for you.” The other thing nobody prepares you for about Palo Alto is how offensively healthy everyone appears to be. You arrive thinking you’re doing reasonably well. Maybe you’ve had a salad recently. Maybe you took a walk on purpose once. Then suddenly you’re standing in line behind a man who is allegedly fifty-two years old but looks like he was assembled in a Scandinavian laboratory last Thursday. Everyone here has the skin of a newborn dolphin. Women in black Lululemon glide past carrying green juice and somehow manage to look both relaxed and aggressively optimized. Men who claim to have “just been slammed with board meetings” still possess the compact musculature of professional cyclists fleeing the Tour de France. Even the dogs look expensive and emotionally regulated. Back home, if you saw a group of middle-aged men jogging shirtless, you assumed there’d been some sort of emergency. Here they travel in organized clusters at six in the morning discussing mitochondrial health and seed oils. One man at Coupa told me he’d “fully eliminated inflammatory inputs.” I didn’t ask what this meant because I was eating banana bread and suddenly felt ashamed. Everywhere I looked, there were men in fleece vests speaking a language that sounded vaguely English but contained no recognizable human emotion. “We’re building tooling around decentralized trust.” “The space is evolving super fast.” “There’s a lot of energy around synthetic cognition.” One man said, “I’m not optimizing for money anymore.” He said this while sitting in front of a laptop that cost four thousand dollars. I rented a tiny apartment near Stanford University and quickly learned that Stanford students travel in packs like very confident gazelles. They move at dangerous speeds on electric scooters while discussing whether consciousness can be uploaded to the cloud. One afternoon, I overheard two undergraduates talking outside the bookstore. “I’m only taking four classes this quarter because my startup’s scaling.” The other one nodded solemnly. “Yeah, burnout is real.” They both looked about fourteen years old. The strangest thing about Palo Alto is that everyone appears to be either: 1. starting a company, 2. selling a company, 3. investing in a company, or 4. recovering emotionally from being insufficiently early to Bitcoin. Even the children seem busy. At a playground near downtown, I heard a father say to his toddler: “Sweetie, use your words. Are you feeling pre-product-market-fit?” The child burst into tears, which honestly felt appropriate. At lunch, people migrate toward Nobu Palo Alto with the determination of spawning salmon. I went there once with a friend who works in venture capital, a profession I still don’t fully understand except that it seems to involve eating expensive sushi while rejecting other people’s dreams. The hostess asked if we had a reservation. My friend smiled. “We know Kevin.” This turned out to be sufficient. Inside, every table contained a conversation that sounded medically concerning. “Our runway’s getting tighter.” “We may need another round.” “He’s pivoting hard.” It was impossible to tell whether these people were discussing startups or emergency aviation procedures. I once met a venture capitalist there who casually informed me he was sixty-one. I laughed because I thought he was joking. He wasn’t. The man looked like a substitute Peloton instructor. His jawline could have sliced sashimi. During dinner he ate approximately four molecules of tuna and spent twenty minutes explaining the anti-inflammatory benefits of Nordic sauna cycles. “I’ve completely cut out alcohol,” he said. Then, after a pause: “Except ceremonial mezcal.” At one point my friend leaned over and whispered, “That’s Sam Altman.” I looked across the room and saw a pale man in a gray sweater drinking sparkling water while listening very intensely. “But that could also just be somebody from product,” I said. “That’s true,” my friend admitted. Celebrity sightings here are uniquely disappointing because everyone already looks like a tech billionaire. Half the men dress like they’ve been evacuated from an REI store. The other half look like they’re on their way to testify before Congress. Once, at Whole Foods, I became convinced I had seen Elon Musk examining avocados. I stared for nearly thirty seconds before realizing it was simply an exhausted father wearing a black jacket and the expression of someone trying to colonize Mars while also remembering to buy oat milk. The social rules here are baffling. People don’t ask where you’re from. They ask: “What are you working on?” And when you answer honestly — “Oh, I’m writing essays” — they react the way Victorians might respond to hearing you collect human teeth. At parties, conversations become competitive in very specific ways. In normal cities, people brag about vacations or home renovations. In Palo Alto, people brag about suffering. “I haven’t slept in three days.” “I forgot to eat yesterday.” “I accidentally took two investor calls during my anniversary dinner.” Everyone laughs proudly, like overworked raccoons. Even illness here sounds competitive. A man at a party told me, “My cortisol was a disaster last quarter.” He said it with the same grim pride my uncle uses when discussing surviving the Blizzard of ’78. One evening I attended a dinner in Atherton at a house so large it had multiple climate zones. The host introduced me to a man who was “doing fascinating work in longevity.” The man looked thirty-five. “I’m actually fifty-eight,” he said. There was a long silence while everyone calculated whether eternal life might be worth hearing the phrase “biohacking journey” every day forever. Around dessert, someone asked if I’d tried cold plunging. I said no. Another guest looked genuinely alarmed. “But then how do you regulate inflammation?” I almost answered, “Catholic guilt,” but I didn’t think they’d understand. There is an exhausting amount of intentionality around the human body here. People don’t merely exercise; they “train for longevity.” They don’t eat lunch; they “optimize glucose response.” A friend invited me to breakfast and then consumed what appeared to be damp bark in a ceramic bowl. “This changed my biomarkers,” he told me. The truly maddening part is that many of these people aren’t actually young. Palo Alto contains a shocking number of fifty-year-olds disguised as thirty-eight-year-olds and thirty-eight-year-olds disguised as graduate students. Everyone has some combination of: * personal trainer * sleep consultant * infrared sauna * standing desk * cold plunge * emotional-support electrolyte packet Meanwhile I eat one blueberry muffin and immediately look like Winston Churchill. The local gym frightened me so badly I canceled my membership after one visit. The locker room resembled an audition for “Succession: Athleisure Edition.” Every man had the same close-cropped haircut and the same compact, efficient body, as though they’d all been designed by Apple. One guy casually mentioned he’d just completed an ultramarathon. Another said: “Oh nice, which one?” As if there were several. I once tried jogging around the Stanford campus and was immediately overtaken by a woman pushing a stroller uphill while calmly discussing a seed-round valuation on AirPods. The stroller contained twins. The twins were eating organic almond butter from reusable bamboo pouches. One of them looked more emotionally resilient than I am. And despite all this optimization, everyone also seems profoundly exhausted. You’ll see some radiant-looking founder with perfect posture and suspiciously white teeth saying things like: “I haven’t slept in four days.” Or: “My WHOOP data says I’m technically deceased.” It creates a strange atmosphere where nobody appears to age normally. The entire town feels suspended in a permanent state of highly funded wellness panic. By midnight, everyone at the Atherton dinner party had become extremely earnest. A venture capitalist explained to me that artificial intelligence would soon eliminate the need for most human labor. “What will people do all day?” I asked. He shrugged. “Found podcasts, probably.” Later, walking home through silent streets full of Teslas charging like sleeping livestock, I passed a young man talking very intensely into his phone. “No, listen,” he said. “It’s Uber, but for emotions.” And the terrible thing was, part of me thought: That’ll probably get funded.”

$EOS.AX If you scroll my profile, you would think I like to do TA. But actually I love doing fundamental analysis as well. I enjoy finding gems and digging through the company just as much as I enjoy the TA. That work takes weeks, and I'm super selective, that's why I don't spam tickers continuously. But when I do put out a thesis, you can bet that I have done the homework. Here is my framework: Question zero: enabler or beneficiary? Before anything else. Does this company build the foundation of the AI buildout, or just use AI to improve a service? Enablers are examples like semis, memory, neoclouds, photonics. The picks and shovels. Beneficiaries are fintech, SaaS, healthcare. Enablers capture the most value right now because they can't be skipped. Demand is outstripping supply. The odds of picking a winner are higher. Beneficiaries fight in crowded markets, and at worst AI eats them. See the recent SaaS bloodbath. Pick enablers to be included in your portfolio want enablers. 1. Leadership. Everything about a company stems from the top, the culture, the finances, the engineering, the technology, the customer relations etc. > Does the founder have experience that actually maps to this company, or a resume from an unrelated field? > How long has the CEO been in the seat? > Is it founder led? > Do they own real stock, and are they buying in the open market or quietly selling? > Any history of missing their own guidance, related party deals, or restatements? And if so, why? Unproven at this scale is fine if the credentials fit and their own money is on the line. Documented dishonesty is an instant fail. 2. Revenue Quality. > Is it recurring, or a one time lump that won't repeat? > Is it spread across many customers, or does one whale carry the whole number and could walk tomorrow? > Where does it come from geographically? One country, or many? Heavy China exposure is a different risk than a diversified base across the US, Europe and Asia. > Does the cash flowing in match the revenue being booked, or is the growth living on paper? 3. Revenue Growth. This is crucial for finding 10 baggers > Is there a credible inflection coming, or just a steady trailing rate? > Is the capex already in the ground to support it? If not there are dilution risks. > Is the customer pipeline named, or hand waved? > Is there any guidance on revenue growth given by management? A flat company with a real inflection ahead beats a steady grower with nothing coming. 4. Moat. The edge that protects them. Extremely important to find winners in the long run as well. > Is it an artificial moat, the Lululemon or Nike kind, built on brand and marketing that a competitor can erode with enough spend? Or is it something only this company can do? > Switching costs, multi year qualification cycles, patents, sole supplier status? > Has anyone with money and reputation on the line validated it? A named hyperscaler, a platform leader, a strategic investor on the board? > External validators are hard evidence, not narrative. Counterparties don't sign off on weak operators. 5. Asymmetry. Risk to reward at today's price. Most people get this backwards. It is not "the stock has run, I missed it." It's "does the upside still pay me for the downside." > What's my floor? Cash on the balance sheet, trust value, book value? > If the bear case hits, how far do I actually fall? > If the thesis works, where does it go? > Does the probability weighted upside still beat the downside by a wide margin? A stock that has 5x'd and still pays you 2 to 1 is more asymmetric than one that has done nothing and pays you 1.3 to 1. There are many ways to value a company, for me, the best way to value growth stocks is looking at their forward earnings/revenues and comparing it to peers. This is what I did with 
$BRUN
 to determine it was undervalued. Find your style. 6. Conviction Gap. The space between what I can prove today and what the next catalysts will prove. > What is genuinely unknown right now? > Which way does the existing evidence lean? > What specific event would convert the unknown into fact? When does that event happen? A wide gap with evidence pointing the right way is the whole game. It means the market is pricing in uncertainty I have a reasoned view on. Thin analyst coverage isn't a red flag here. It's the opportunity. I write the bear case out in full and pick at it before I ever post. If I can't convince myself first, I won't try to convince you. To summarise 0. AI Enabler over beneficiary. 1. Leadership I trust. 2. Real revenue. 3. Forward growth. 4. A moat only they can build/is hard to replicate. 5. Asymmetry that pays me. 6. A gap with a catalyst to close it. You can take these 6 criteria to come up with a composite score to decide whether you want to decide to invest in the company or not. 7. How I integrate TA into all of this. The fundamentals tell me what to buy. The technicals tell me when. The best setup is when both line up. Great fundamentals with a broken chart just means you bag hold while you wait, sometimes for years even! See 
$PATH
. Arguably the right company, sadly the wrong tape. And this is huge opportunity cost. So once a name clears my framework, I check the chart for confluence. > Is the stock breaking out of a downtrend or a long consolidation? > Are the EMAs stacked bullish, shorter over longer, all sloping up? > Is there real volume driving the move, or is it drifting on nothing? Each one on its own may be noise, but stacked together, they can be a signal. That confluence is the difference between catching the entry and riding the wave, or being early and bleeding. If you've not seen ALO takeover of the French Riviera, you've been living under a rock. A 72-metre yacht moored in Cannes Bay during the Film Festival. Pilates and meditation at sea. Sail to Monaco for the Grand Prix. 40 branded sunbeds on the Hôtel Martinez pier. This is a brand that started as activewear in 2007. Most marketing teams will look at this and try to extract the playbook. They'll over-engineer it into a 50-slide deck on omnichannel brand-building strategy. I'm going to oversimplify it. The cleanest way to build brand equity is to tie yourself to something already cool. Then... remove the other cool thing. The Riviera in May is already culturally loaded. Cannes Film Festival. Monaco Grand Prix. The exact stretch of coastline where luxury has been performed for a hundred years. Alo didn't create any of that. They plan to stand next to it for a few weeks and let the proximity do the work. When the yacht leaves Monaco, the Grand Prix is over, and the Film Festival wraps, the "cool" stays attached to the brand. The aesthetic carries forward. The footage circulates on socials for the next 12 months. New customers who never saw the activation in person still associate Alo with the kind of life that includes private yachts and Riviera mornings. That's the trick. ⚑ You don't have to manufacture cool. You borrow it. ⚑ You don't have to explain why you belong in that environment. You just show up enough times that the question stops getting asked. ⚑ You spend a fraction on activations next to things people already care about. Look at what other brands have done with the same playbook. Lululemon at the marathon majors. Liquid Death at music festivals and skateparks. White Claw at college spring break. Same principle. For most consumer brands, the lesson is simple. Stop trying to be the source of the cool. Instead: 1. Find what is considered "cool" for your target audience. 2. Work out how to show up there. 3. Do it again, and again, and again. Find where the cool already lives, plant your flag near it, and let association do the compounding.

Impulse Wave: (1-2-3-4-5) Wave 1: The initial move in the trend direction (smart money buys early). Wave 2: Pullback (prices retrace, but don’t go below the start of Wave 1). Wave 3: The strongest and longest move (mass adoption of the trend). Wave 4: Another correction, often weaker than Wave 2. Wave 5: Final push in the trend direction (fueled by FOMO). Corrective Wave (A-B-C): Wave A: Price goes against the trend. Wave B: Partial retracement (people think trend will continue). Wave C: Final move down, completing the correction. If not there are dilution risks. > Is the customer pipeline named, or hand waved? > Is there any guidance on revenue growth given by management? A flat company with a real inflection ahead beats a steady grower with nothing coming. 4. Moat. The edge that protects them. Extremely important to find winners in the long run as well. > Is it an artificial moat, the Lululemon or Nike kind, built on brand and marketing that a competitor can erode with enough spend? : Quick Thoughts On Chip Wilson’s Win Don’t normally take victory laps but this one feels exceptionally good. The vast majority of Wall Street thought Chip had no chance in his proxy battle with Lululemon (“maybe he gets one”) – almost to the point of frustration he would even dare to engage in it. Elliott has been radio silent ever since their candidate for CEO was dismissed (another example of Wall Street collectively getting it wrong as most sell-siders were positive it would be Jane Nielsen). Yet rather than just opining from thin air like most others, we did the work. Four extensive notes (46 pages in total) that Wall Street would never write as dug deeply into this specific proxy battle. Numerous discussions with former CEO Christine Day (who went through these issues during her own tenure). All augmented by our extensive decade+ pre-existing knowledge of the company as a former sell-side analyst. This is what real independent research looks like and the perfect example of what we are building at M Squared Capital. We thank our Angel Subscribers for their patience as we focused on this subject. Tough to be a Lululemon bear right now. The largest overhang to the story has been removed. Management almost certainly sandbagged next week’s earnings for optics heading into what they expected to be a proxy battle later next month. Operationally things are not great (we know the data shows that too), but they also aren’t terrible (total revenue still positive). And the company has 12% of its market cap sitting in cash with enough room on its share repurchase authorization to use it all (not to mention a HSD FCF yield). This deal with Chip Wilson is probably the best possible outcome for long-term shareholders at this moment. The depressed valuation of Lululemon reflects a narrative that either this noisy battle would continue for years to come, or the incumbent Board is poised to run the company into the ground. The former is taken off the table, and the latter seems less likely with these new additions (particularly Marc Maurer). We had previously speculated that Lululemon might be acquired should this situation persist. We would have been dismayed to sell our shares below cost in that situation as fully recognize the long-term value of this company. Yet we probably would have voted yes to a transaction as have lost all confidence in the incumbent Board to realize that value. At the end of the day, we understand why the incumbent Board thought they had a leg to stand on: other than the stock price, things really aren’t that bad at Lululemon. Yet. Last year they ate a bigger impact from tariffs than almost any other company (due to de minimis) and still delivered ~20% EBIT margins on MSD revenue growth. But we also understand Chip’s point of view that this is the reason why change can still occur before the brand is impaired past the point of no return. Another year in the current direction and it’s quite possible that nothing could be done to fix the business for a very long time. For the first time this year investors can be reasonably optimistic about this story. The announcement of Heidi O’Neill as CEO clearly didn’t provide that optimism but even she benefits from some of this whitewashing. It’s also nice to see language from Marti Morfitt that the company needs to clear a path forward for Heidi. Unsure if included in the final agreement but we note Reuters mentioned yesterday that Chip will have access to Heidi on a regular basis. This should end any speculation that Heidi will be pushed out and at this point the company needs to use all resources necessary to ensure her tenure begins on a high note to repair damage caused by this unfortunate and poorly managed (from a corporate governance perspective) battle. However, we recommend that the company takes no actions that risk breaking her non-compete agreement with 
$NKE
 (such as the town hall she hosted a few weeks ago), to ensure that yet another crisis does not follow the conclusion of this one. The main thing that remains to be seen is who will step off the incumbent Board to make way for Chip’s two current nominees and a nominee to be named later this year. We assume Marti Morfitt will be the member that steps down later this year as the company still needs her to oversee as Executive Chair until Heidi joins in September. Highly difficult to see her surviving this deal given her extremely long tenure at the company and poor decision to engage in the proxy battle that ultimately gave Chip what he wanted to begin with (three Board seats). We are looking forward to seeing how much this proxy battle costs the company as it certainly seems they spared no expense engaging in it. We are less concerned with the donation to Kitsilano Beach to cover Chip’s expenses given the company’s long-standing history in that area (birthplace, SeaWheeze Half Marathon, etc) but that also is coming out of the pockets of shareholders. We wonder whose brand benefits most from that donation, Lululemon or Chip Wilson, given that Chip already has a day named after him in Vancouver (October 3rd is “Summer and Chip Wilson Day”).

Common take: Canadian companies don't buy from startups because they're risk-averse. I've sold to Canadian banks, retailers, grocers & pharmacy chains as a startup for 20 years. The description is accurate -- it really does suck to sell to Canadian businesses as a startup. But the reason is wrong. As a startup you're rarely selling just a solution -- you're selling a paradigm shift ("you run a custom ecommerce engine, but SaaS changes what's possible"). So the real ask is: adopt an unproven paradigm AND trust a small startup to deliver it. Now picture the typical Canadian buyer: a company that's rarely #1 in its field, comfortable in its position, with a decision-maker promoted on tenure -- not for being a maverick. The ones who DO take paradigm risks (Lululemon, Shopify) do it because reinvention is core to their identity. They're the exception. It's not that Canadian enterprises prefer US vendors. It's that if they're going to bet on a new paradigm, a small startup won't be the one to convince them -- but an OpenAI, SAP, or Salesforce will. There's something deeper underneath it too. Across art, science, and tech, Canadians rarely see themselves as the ones who define the next wave -- so they don't trust homegrown talent to do it either. We instinctively look elsewhere for the future.

The reason this looks silly as diversification is that it isn't. A company that buys a coffee machine isn't diversifying into competing with Starbucks, a bank that gives you a pen isn't getting into the pen business, a salesperson who takes a client out to a nice dinner isn't competing with the restaurant. Your cost numbers don't really make sense; the only cost they have is to put up a website and buy some inventory from one of the many commodity suppliers of clothes. I don't think that every school that puts their logo on a sweatshirt had to pull $100m from the endowment first! My guess is that the goal is similar to Costco hot dogs and Ikea meatballs, i.e. it's hard to know whether a given mortgage is a good deal, but if you can buy 85%-of-Lululemon-quality at half the price, that is something people can anchor to. People talk about clothes a lot more than financial services lead-gen companies, and for a lot longer—a shirt is relevant as long as you own it, whereas if you're talking about the mortgage you got years after the fact, it's probably because rates have gone up since then, not because you simply can't stop thinking about what an incredible lead-gen experience you had. (Except me: I do have a funny lead-gen experience that's more interesting than the mortgage rate. But I'm speaking generally.) This kind of thing—company swag, perks, selling hard-to-value products while subsidizing or giving away more legible ones—is common enough that companies stand out when they don't do it. People argue over which airline has the best service, but they tend to agree that Ryanair has the worst, because Ryanair has embraced that reputation for being too cheap to hire friendly people. It's a marketing schtick! I think the only notable thing here is that, as mentioned above, banks often buy fancy pens, and they seem to buy them with the goal that 1) you will get that pen because you physically visited the bank, which is revenue-accretive for them in a way that swamps the marginal cost of a nice-ish pen, and 2) they're hoping it turns out to be the nicest pen you have, so you'll use it by default and constantly flash their logo everywhere. (Note that the cohort of people who often sign documents, and who generally have a pen with them, is more valuable to a bank than the people who don't.) You can't understand financial services without contemplating just how hard it is to sell "a stream of cash flows between you and a counterparty based on the passage of time or some specific conditions" versus making a TV ad for, say, a pizza. It's hard to visualize, so financial services companies license characters (Metlife Snoopy), invent them (GEICO Gecko), convert them from one-offs to recurring franchises (Progressive Flo), etc. Banks pay to put customized buildings in expensive locations even though those buildings will be mostly empty of customers most of the time. Financial lead-gen is so valuable that you can make a fortune selling used cars at a loss, entirely because you get paid for introducing the car buyer to an auto lender. This produces some informatively counterintuitive decisions.
