Here's the actual list, organized by how "bootstrapped" they really were — there's a meaningful difference between "never took a dollar" and "raised one small round after proving the model." Tier 1: Never took venture capital (or took it only as a partial exit), reached $1B+ Mailchimp — Ben Chestnut and Dan Kurzius bootstrapped from a web design consultancy starting 2001. Sold to Intuit for $12B in 2021, largest bootstrapped exit ever. Never took outside investment. Zoho — Sridhar Vembu started in 1996, fully bootstrapped, ~$1.4B annual revenue with 100M+ users. Valued at ~$12.4B (2024 Hurun report). Has consistently turned down VC. Patagonia — Yvon Chouinard bootstrapped from selling climbing gear out of his car. Estimated $3B+ valuation; in 2022 transferred ownership to a trust dedicated to fighting climate change rather than selling or IPOing. Basecamp / 37signals — Jason Fried and DHH have been profitable for 25+ years, never took VC, multiple successful products. Founders' net worths in the hundreds of millions each; company valuation not public but estimates run $1B+. Craigslist — Craig Newmark deliberately kept the company lean. Estimated worth in the billions based on revenue (~$1B/year at peak), but he's resisted commercial expansion. Implied valuation easily $1B+. Valve — Gabe Newell self-funded with proceeds from his Microsoft stock. Estimated $10B+ valuation via Steam dominance. No outside investment. Epic Games — Tim Sweeney started in his parents' basement in 1991. Now valued at $30B+ after Fortnite. Took late strategic investment from Tencent and Sony, but the foundation was bootstrapped for ~20 years. Spanx — Sara Blakely started with $5,000 in savings in 2000. Bootstrapped for 21 years until Blackstone took majority in 2021 at $1.2B valuation. Blakely became a billionaire. Tier 2: Started with personal savings or credit cards (<$50K), eventually took VC after proving the model Atlassian — Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar started 2002 with $10K AUD on credit cards. No VC for 8 years and 40 consecutive profitable quarters. Now ~$40B market cap (NASDAQ: TEAM). Wayfair — Niraj Shah and Steve Conine started with $7K in 2002. Profitable in their first month, no VC until they hit $500M in revenue. Peak $40B, currently ~$6B post-correction. GitHub — Three co-founders bootstrapped from 2008-2012 before raising $100M from a16z. Sold to Microsoft for $7.5B in 2018. GoPro — Nick Woodman started with $10K from selling necklaces with his wife. IPO'd at $11B peak valuation, currently smaller after the action camera market commoditized. Yeti — Roy and Ryan Seiders bootstrapped from making fishing rods. IPO'd at $1.7B in 2018, currently ~$3B. Pluralsight — Aaron Skonnard bootstrapped for years before Insight Partners came in. Sold to Vista Equity for $3.5B in 2021. Calendly — Tope Awotona invested his life savings as part of a $550K seed round, remained capital-efficient for 7 years. Last valued at $3B in 2021. Shutterstock — Jon Oringer started with his own savings and his own photographs. Currently ~$2B market cap. SurveyMonkey — Ryan Finley bootstrapped from 1999, sold to Spectrum Equity in 2009. Was a unicorn at 2018 IPO, currently ~$1B+. Topgolf — Started bootstrapped 2000s, eventually took strategic investment. Now ~$4B+ as part of Topgolf Callaway. ZipRecruiter — Ian Siegel and team bootstrapped as a "lifestyle business" before raising $63M Series A. IPO'd 2021 at ~$2.4B, currently smaller. NerdWallet — Tim Chen bootstrapped 2009-2015 before $64M Series A. IPO'd 2021 around $1.3B. Campaign Monitor — Sydney-based, bootstrapped to scale before a $250M first round from Insight Venture Partners — the first-round size is the tell of how much they'd built on their own. Some legendary "almost bootstrapped" worth knowing: Lululemon — Chip Wilson started with personal savings in 1998. Now ~$35B market cap. Did some early strategic capital but no traditional VC path. Stripe — Often gets called bootstrapped but actually took early YC and angel funding (~$2M seed). Not strictly bootstrapped. WhatsApp — Took some early Sequoia investment but extremely capital-efficient. Sold to Facebook for $19B. Borderline. Patterns worth pulling out, given your serial-entrepreneur context: A few things this list reveals that's relevant for the ParkOS thinking: B2B SaaS dominates the truly bootstrapped tier. Mailchimp, Zoho, Atlassian, Basecamp, Calendly, Pluralsight, Campaign Monitor — recurring revenue businesses with low marginal cost are the most capital-efficient model in history. ParkOS fits this template structurally. The bootstrapped path consistently produces higher founder equity at exit. Wayfair's founders held substantial stakes at $40B peak. Atlassian's founders are still ~30% owners after IPO. Mailchimp's founders split $12B essentially intact. VC dilution typically leaves founders with 10-15% at IPO; bootstrappers often hold 40-70%+. The "no VC for X years" pattern is more common than "never any VC." Most of these companies eventually took some capital — but did so from a position of strength (already profitable, already at scale) which dramatically shifted the terms in founders' favor. The discipline is in when you take capital, not whether you ever do. Vertical-specific software + services (Yeti for outdoor, Spanx for shapewear, Patagonia for outdoor apparel) shows you don't need to be pure tech to bootstrap to billion-dollar scale. Operations-heavy businesses with strong brand equity work too. The clear common thread: all of these companies were profitable early and grew on customer revenue rather than investor capital. Educational Note Of The Day Why "first hour reversals" happen so often after big gap moves When markets gap up significantly at the open (like NQ +1.6% yesterday), the first hour of cash trading frequently sees a reversal or significant pullback. Here's why: 1. Overnight gaps come from futures, not real volume.A gap up of 200+ NQ points is built on relatively thin overnight liquidity. When New York opens at 9:30 AM ET, you suddenly have institutional desks, ETF rebalancing, options market makers, and retail flow ALL hitting the tape at once. The thin gap meets thick volume — and the gap often gets challenged. 2. Gap fade is a real strategy.There are entire institutional desks built around fading opening gaps. The data supports them: roughly 60-65% of gap-ups above 1% see at least a partial fill in the first 60 minutes of cash trading. 3. Overnight news has time to be re-evaluated. At 5 AM CT, you reacted to Trump's tweet emotionally. By 9 AM, smarter desks have read the fine print, considered Iran's official response, checked oil's behavior, and decided whether to chase or fade. That reassessment process IS the morning reversal. The trading framework: Strong gap + strong volume on the open + holds above pre-market high in first 5 minutes = trend day up, lean long Strong gap + weak volume on the open + immediately rejects pre-market high = fade likely, lean short the bounce Strong gap + chop in first 15 minutes = wait, no edge The lesson from yesterday's tape: the bounce held into the close, which means today's gap-up at 9:30 is starting from a stronger foundation than yesterday's was. Yesterday was a coin-flip reversal risk. Today the trend bias is stronger.

 last week on its real estate monetization plans: Earlier this year CEO Gary Friedman teased that RH would sell ~$500 MM of its owned real estate over the next 2 years to pay down debt Several months later RH has yet to sell real estate—but did take an important step toward future sales last month when it reorganized the ownership of several Aspen, CO properties that it had owned with a JV partner RH received ~$50 MM in cash and $10 MM in non-cash capital contributions and its JV partner took full ownership of the majority of Aspen development sites that had been co-owned in the JV RH also secured outright ownership of the RH Aspen Guesthouse property that is in development and used part of the $50 MM in cash to repay $32 MM in property level debt RH also has full ownership of multiple Aspen buildings that are leased to tenants such as Chanel, Gucci, and lululemon RH now has full control of 4 of its owned galleries that it may seek to monetize via sale leaseback including RH England and 3 recently opened galleries in Indianapolis, Cleveland and Detroit The Company also has 3 owned development-stage sites (involving locations in CA, NJ and Europe) The next step to monetize the real estate? The market is reading one number (flat total revenue) and missing the rotation happening underneath it. TL;DR: At ~$105 and ~10x earnings, LULU is valued as a structural loser, but China is compounding ~20% and quietly becoming the growth engine. My read leans contrarian-long, with the catch that the US has to stop bleeding for the math to work. The headline looks dead: FY guidance cut to flat-to-down, US comps negative, EPS well off last year. That is the story everyone is pricing. But composition is doing something the aggregate hides. China grew 23% in constant currency last quarter and is now ~19% of revenue, up from 16% a year ago. A 20%-compounder taking share of the mix from a saturated US base re-accelerates blended growth on its own, and the headline never warns you in advance. The real question into the ~Sept 3 print is margin, not demand. Tariffs and markdowns are the live wound, with management guiding a steep gross-margin step-down. If the US merely stabilizes while China keeps its pace, the 10x multiple is pricing a decline that the mix shift is already arresting. Kill condition: China comps decelerate toward the teens, or US comps deepen instead of flattening. Then it is just a cheap stock that deserves to be cheap. For information, not instruction.

It's a bit of a game. Signing bonuses are the real moneymaker, but you don't want too many open/closes. So you need a no-fee card with each provider first, and it needs a year of history ideally. Then you get a high-fee-high-signing-bonus card. Enjoy the benefits, hit the bonus. Use the benefits in your first year. Then transfer the line of credit to your same-company no-fee card and close the fee card. Rinse and repeat. Companies have a 5-year cooldown time and there are at least 12 meaningfully-high-rewards-and-bonuses cards, so you can grab a few thousand in signing bonuses (plus actual normal usage rewards) every six months. Key is: transfer the line of credit to a longstanding low-but-not-zero-usage no-fee card, so over time you begin to have a massive amount of available credit and, correspondingly, a comically low utilization rate. This makes companies even gladder to have you, and you get more/better signing offers.

The other key is use your benefits. We're on a round of Amex Platinum maxxing right now, and it has loads of random tertiary benefits (lululemon credit? restaurant credit? airline upgrade fee credit?). Use them. People often let their benefits sit idle. But they're use-or-less benefits! Don't do date night to any restaurant; do date night at the restaurant your credit card will give you $100 cash back on. Don't stay at whichever hotel on vacation. Stay at the one, and book via the method, that actually gets you big points bonuses and status perks. You have to be willing to constrain and modify your choices. Many people won't.

#Storytime My first small business was a gas station. It was in a small town and the only gas station in the county. It was a Mobil station, business was great and I had pricing power. If people needed gas, they came to me. The pumps stayed busy, the store stayed busy and margins held up because there wasn't another option. A few years later, some guy opened a no name gas station about half a mile down the road. From that point on, my business was never the same. Nothing changed about demand. People still needed gas. Nothing changed about my product. I was still selling branded fuel. The only thing that changed was supply. Customers suddenly had another option. Competition increased. Pricing power disappeared. I had to compete instead of dictate. The reason I'm telling this story now is when I made that post about AAPL x DRAM, I was the bad guy. It doesn't matter how good your product is. Uber's IPO was led by a banker who moonlighted for years as an Uber driver. Sometimes, these tactics include brutally sacrificing fees to get your name attached to a big listing and build relationships, specially if you're not a large and famous Wall Street bank. The SBI Funds Management IPO paid just 0.05% of its issue size to bankers, compared to the average of 1.86% for IPOs last year. That's ~₹4.6 crore split among 9 banks - ₹50 lakh each. The similar-sized ICICI Prudential AMC IPO recently paid bankers ₹187.67 crore - 1.8% of its size. Low fees is standard for government company listings, but banks jump on in the hope of being hired on well-paying future deals (acquisitions, debt offerings). The 6 banks on SBI's ₹25,000 crore QIP last year were paid a token ₹1 each. Personally, I'd rather wear the tights.

Costco regulars knowing the difference strengthens Costco's defense, but it doesn't erase the claim if broader evidence of potential confusion exists. how marketers kill brands: nobody sets out to do it, but most brands follow this pathway: find a niche position it hard build a fanbase expand the product soften the message so no one's left out bonus (if they're smart): go back to the original messaging and repeat. the first four steps build something people love, then step five throws it all away. the problem is that it never feels like a mistake. the revenue's up, shareholders wants more, someone tells you that you're too narrow in your focus and leaving money on the table, so you widen the door to find more revenue which results in you stop being for someone and start being for anyone who'll pay. lululemon spent years being the brand for aspirational yoga women, now those women are in alo and lululemon "stands for wellness," whatever that's meant to mean. nike built the whole thing on serious athletes, now the runners with taste have moved to hoka or on. the product's still fine, it's the meaning that went thin, and once the meaning's thin the door's wide open, so alo and on and hoka just walk in, happy to be for someone whilst you're busy trying to be for everyone. the thing big brands forget and small ones survive on: you can sell the product to everyone, but the messaging still has to be for someone. patagonia gets bought by bankers who'll never spend a night outside, doesn't matter, it's still made for the bloke halfway up a rock face at 6am. the banker isn't buying a jacket, he's buying a bit of that world, and the second you water the branding down to include him he stops buying, because now there's nothing left to buy into. growing the product grows the business, growing the message just turns you into a logo nobody feels anything about. so before you soften anything, work out who you're actually softening it for, nine times out of ten it isn't the customer, it's a spreadsheet. which brand do you reckon "grew" its way into meaning nothing? i'll go first.

I used to hear people say that in developed countries, things often cost the same number as they do in China, just in a different currency. I never really understood what they meant, but after moving to Australia, I’ve realized that it’s often true. IKEA delivery costs 89 yuan in China—and 89 Australian dollars here. When ordering groceries online, a shopping bag might cost 2 yuan in China—and 2 dollars here. A bus ride costs a few yuan in China—and 2.80 dollars here. A bottle of Coke from a convenience store costs around 4 yuan in China—and about 4 dollars here. A normal taxi ride in China might cost anywhere from the teens to just over 30 yuan. In Australia, it’s often roughly the same number in Australian dollars. One Australian dollar is about 4.72 yuan. The minimum hourly wage in Australia is around 26 dollars, while in Shanghai it’s around 25 yuan. An ordinary person here might earn a little over 4,000 Australian dollars a month, which is numerically similar to what some people earn in parts of China. The main difference is that almost anything involving human labour is very expensive in Australia, while mass-produced goods are genuinely cheap relative to local incomes. An ordinary person might earn over 4,000 dollars a month, but the latest iPhone only costs around one or two thousand—roughly half a month’s salary. Groceries such as meat, eggs and dairy cost about the same number as they do in Shanghai, but to me, the quality often feels better than what I used to buy from Hema or Dingdong. The eggs here are especially good. Fruit and vegetable prices depend on the category. Some are similar to Shanghai, while others are extremely expensive. A coffee in Shanghai costs around 25–30 yuan. Here, it costs around 5–7 Australian dollars. Again, the number is fairly similar, but relative to Australian wages, coffee is incredibly cheap. Eating out is another story. A simple meal costs around 15–20 dollars. Converted into yuan, that’s about 70–95 yuan, which feels very expensive. I haven’t had much experience yet with home repairs, cleaning services or healthcare, but I assume anything involving professional labour will be extremely expensive. So far, I’ve found two things that are cheaper than in China. The first is milk. It’s not only cheaper, but noticeably better-tasting. The second is Lululemon. Something that costs around 1,000 yuan in China might cost the equivalent of only 600–700 yuan here. I’m sure there are more. I’ll keep looking.

On the night of March 11, 2011, two employees finished closing the Lululemon store in Bethesda, Maryland. Earlier that evening, Jayna Murray had reported coworker Brittany Norwood to a manager after allegedly discovering stolen merchandise in her bag. A short time later, Norwood asked Murray to return to the store, claiming she had forgotten her wallet inside. Murray went back and never came out. The following morning, a store manager discovered a horrifying scene. The store appeared to have been ransacked, Jayna Murray was found dead, and Brittany Norwood was located bound inside a restroom. Norwood initially told investigators that two masked men had broken into the store, assaulted them, and murdered Murray before leaving her alive. Investigators quickly found that the evidence did not support her account. There were no signs of intruders, no forensic evidence to support the alleged assault, and the physical evidence inside the store contradicted Norwood's story. The medical examiner determined that Murray had suffered an extraordinarily violent attack involving multiple weapons and numerous defensive injuries, indicating she had fought desperately to survive. Within days, Brittany Norwood was arrested and charged with first-degree murder. In 2012, she was convicted and sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Prosecutors argued that the killing began after Murray confronted Norwood over shoplifting, making it one of the most shocking workplace homicides in recent American history. Anybody can shoplift in California- Proposition 47 (2014) raised the felony theft threshold from $400 to $950 and created the specific misdemeanor shoplifting statute, aiming to reduce incarceration for low-level property crimes. Rising organized retail theft and smash-and-grab incidents led voters to pass Proposition 36 in November 2024 and the Legislature to enact a bipartisan package of laws effective in 2025 that restored stronger tools against repeat offenders and organized rings while leaving ordinary first-time low-value shoplifting as a misdemeanor. Enforcement and charging decisions still vary by county and district attorney. First-time cases frequently resolve through diversion, deferred entry of judgment, civil compromise, or informal probation rather than jail time. A conviction can later be expunged under PC 1203.4 after successful completion of probation or sentence. Meanwhile- a clear pattern of policies, legislation, and cultural framing has made intervening against shoplifters professionally and socially risky for ordinary retail workers. Corporate “Observe and Report” Policies Major retailers (Walmart, Target, Lululemon, Circle K, Dollar General, and many others) maintain strict “do not confront / do not chase / do not touch” rules for non-security staff. Employees who physically intervene, follow thieves out of the store, or even engage verbally can be—and have been—fired. Notable examples: • Lululemon fired two Georgia employees in 2023 after they engaged suspected robbers (one filmed the incident). The CEO publicly defended the firings, stating employees put themselves and others “in harm’s way” and that “it’s only merchandise.” • A long-time Circle K clerk in Colorado was fired for confronting a knife-wielding shoplifter under the company’s “Don’t Confront and Chase” policy; she later sued. • Similar firings and discipline have occurred at Walmart and other chains. Companies cite legitimate concerns: employee injury or death, civil liability if force is used, and insurance costs. The practical effect is that most frontline workers are instructed to watch, call loss prevention or police, and let the merchandise walk. California Legislative Angle In 2023, the California Senate passed SB 553 (Sen. Dave Cortese), signed by Governor Newsom and effective July 1, 2024. The law requires employers to create workplace violence prevention plans and prohibits them from requiring employees to confront active shoplifters or active threats. It does not make voluntary intervention illegal, but critics (including the California Retailers Association) argued it further discourages any intervention and signals that confrontation is treated primarily as a worker-safety hazard rather than a legitimate defense of property. Cultural and Media Framing Some progressive commentary and advocacy groups frame physical intervention by store employees or security as disproportionate, potentially racist, or an escalation of violence. Narratives often emphasize: • “It’s only merchandise” (insured and replaceable). • Claims that retail theft is exaggerated or over-sensationalized. • Scrutiny of force used by loss-prevention staff, especially in cases involving demographic differences between the employee/security and the suspect. Viral videos of employees stopping thieves sometimes trigger online pile-ons accusing the worker of vigilantism, aggression, or racial profiling. At the same time, many ordinary people and polls show majority support for employees who try to stop theft and opposition to companies punishing them. Legal Reality vs. Practical Reality California still recognizes shopkeeper’s privilege (Penal Code § 490.5). Merchants and their employees may detain a person for a reasonable time and in a reasonable manner if they have probable cause the person is shoplifting. Nike and Lululemon both got sued this week for fake discounts, a "was" price the product barely sold at. The lawsuit is the cheap part. What a permanent discount actually costs you is the expensive one. A quick caveat: these are allegations, not verdicts, and both will argue their pricing was lawful. But the mechanism I care about does not care who wins in court. A discount that never turns off is not a promotion. It is a training program. The first time a customer sees "$98, now $59," the $98 does the work. The tenth time, they learn the only number that was ever real is $59, and your full price is fiction. That trains a specific customer to your brand. Discount-native, lowest lifetime value, least loyal, first to leave the moment someone else is a dollar cheaper. Your front-end ROAS looks great because cheap converts. Your repeat rate quietly erodes, and the soft P&L shows up two quarters later with no single decision to blame. It costs you at the exit too. Any serious buyer runs cohort analysis in diligence, and revenue that rides on an always-on markdown gets haircut in the multiple. And it moves your floor. A permanent discount is a permanent margin cut, so your break-even MER relocates to a worse number and never comes back down, while most brands leave their ROAS targets exactly where they were. The uncomfortable part. If your product only converts with a fake anchor next to it, that is not a pricing tactic. It is an offer problem wearing a creative costume, and no amount of ad testing fixes it. Two questions for your own site. Did the product actually sell at the "was" price in the last 90 days? And what is the always-on version of this sale teaching the people it brings you? Full breakdown in today's article.
